videos.script: Here are twelve orders from Horta, a small online grocer. Each row is one order. Each column records one thing about it: where it went, how it was paid, how many items, what it cost, how long the delivery took. {{table}} Before you compute anything, ask one question of every column. What kind of thing is in it? {{question}} Some columns hold names. Cambuí, Taquaral, pix, card. You can count them, and that is about all. {{names}} Others hold quantities. Eighty-six reais and forty centavos. Thirty-four and a half minutes. Here the arithmetic means something, and a total or an average tells you about the shop. {{quantities}} And some columns hold numbers that are really names. A postcode is written in digits, and its average is a number that describes nothing. {{postcode}} Getting this wrong does not produce an error. A spreadsheet will average a postcode without complaint. That is why the question comes first, before any formula. {{spreadsheet}} By the end of this lesson you will sort any column into one of two families, and you will know what each family lets you do. {{families}}
